query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, the evolution of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior is governed by the redistribution and transformation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases into more stable phases, which alters the alloy's surface chemistry and passive film formation dynamics.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a density below 6 g/cm3, containing a mixture of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal exposure at high temperatures to induce phase transformations and redistribution of Mg-rich intermetallics.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure at temperatures between 400°C and 600°C for varying durations (e.g., 1–10 hours) in an oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Redistribution and transformation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases into more stable phases.
generation.mechanism: Thermal exposure promotes diffusion and phase transformations, leading to the stabilization of less reactive phases and changes in the composition and structure of the surface oxide layer. This affects the alloy's ability to resist corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance will improve after thermal exposure due to the formation of a more stable and protective surface oxide layer, with the extent of improvement depending on the duration and temperature of exposure.
generation.baseline: Initial corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior of the non-equilibrium alloy prior to thermal exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm3 and processed under non-equilibrium conditions. It assumes that the thermal exposure does not lead to complete melting or catastrophic degradation of the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The specific phase transformations and their kinetics, as well as the exact composition and protective properties of the resulting oxide layer, are not fully predictable without experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose samples of the alloy to controlled thermal treatments at 400°C, 500°C, and 600°C for 1, 5, and 10 hours in an oxidizing atmosphere. Measure changes in phase composition using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and evaluate corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance using electrochemical tests and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), respectively.
measurements: Phase composition before and after thermal exposure (XRD, SEM)
Corrosion resistance (electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarization)
High-temperature oxidation resistance (TGA, oxide layer characterization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant changes in phase composition or surface oxide properties are observed after thermal exposure, or if corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance do not improve or worsen, the hypothesis will be falsified.
